hello.title: Hello, Bash
hello.summary: Write your first Bash script, print text with echo and printf, and learn how to run a script.
hello.lesson.0: **Bash** is a shell: a program that reads commands and runs them. You can type commands in a terminal, one at a time, or save them in a text file. Such a file is a **script**. Bash runs its commands from top to bottom. The command `echo` prints its arguments, followed by a new line.
hello.lesson.2: The first line, `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, is the **shebang**. `#!` tells the system which program runs the file, and `/usr/bin/env bash` finds the `bash` program on your computer. Write it as the very first line of every script.
hello.lesson.4: Save the script in a file, for example `hello.sh`. In the terminal, run it with `bash hello.sh`. You can also make the file executable once with `chmod +x hello.sh` and then start it with `./hello.sh`. The `./` means: the file in the current folder.
hello.lesson.5: The next examples leave out the shebang line to keep them short. Put it at the top of your own scripts.
hello.lesson.7: Bash splits a command into words at spaces. `echo` prints its words with one space between them, so extra spaces disappear. Quotes keep text together exactly as written: double quotes `"..."` or single quotes `'...'`.
hello.lesson.9: `echo -n` prints without the new line at the end, so the next output continues on the same line. `echo` without arguments prints an empty line. `;` separates two commands on one line. `#` starts a **comment**: Bash ignores the rest of the line.
hello.lesson.12: `printf` prints text in a format. It does not add a new line, so you write `\n` where a line should end. In the format, `%s` is a placeholder for a string and `%d` for a whole number. The values follow the format. With more values than placeholders, `printf` repeats the format.
hello.card.0: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is the first line of a script (shebang)
hello.card.1: `echo "text"` prints a line, `echo -n` prints without a new line
hello.card.4: `#` starts a comment, `;` separates two commands
hello-1.prompt: What is the first line of a script, `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, called?
hello-1.explain: `#!` at the very start of a file is the shebang. It tells the system which program runs the script.
hello-2.explain: Without quotes, Bash splits the line into words, and `echo` prints them with one space between them.
hello-3.explain: The first `%s` becomes `a`, the second `%s` becomes `b`, and `\n` ends the line.
hello-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Loading...done on one line.
hello-4.explain: `echo -n` does not print the new line at the end, so `done` follows on the same line.
hello-5.explain: `#` starts a comment. Bash ignores `# B`, so `echo` gets only `A`.
hello-6.prompt: Build a line that prints Ada is 36 with printf.
hello-6.explain: The format comes first, then the values in the order of the placeholders: `%s` gets `Ada`, `%d` gets `36`.
hello-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so the script prints Start, then Hello, Bash on one line, then End.
hello-7.explain: Bash runs the lines from top to bottom. `echo -n` prints `Hello, ` without a new line, so `Bash` follows on the same line.
hello-8.prompt: Match each command with what it does.
hello-8.pairs.0: prints its arguments and a new line
hello-9.prompt: This script should print Hello and World on two lines. Which line has the bug?
hello-9.explain: `echo -n` leaves out the new line, so the script prints `HelloWorld`. Write `echo "Hello"`.
hello-10.explain: `;` runs both commands. The first `echo -n` prints `ab` without a new line, and `cd` follows directly.
hello-11.prompt: Complete the script so that ./hello.sh can run the new file.
hello-11.explain: `chmod +x` makes the file executable. Only then can you start it with `./hello.sh`.
hello-12.prompt: This script should print Start, Middle and End. Which line has the bug?
hello-12.explain: The closing quote is missing, so Bash reaches the end of the file inside the text and stops with an error. Write `echo "End"`.
variables.title: Variables
variables.summary: Store values in variables, use quotes correctly, catch the output of commands and calculate with whole numbers.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** stores a value under a name. Write `name=value` to create it. There must be **no spaces** around `=`. To use the value, write `$` before the name: `$name`.
variables.lesson.2: `name = "Ada"` with spaces is an error. Bash then thinks that `name` is a command with the arguments `=` and `Ada`. You get the error `name: command not found`.
variables.lesson.3: `${name}` is the same as `$name`. The braces show where the name ends. You need them when letters or digits follow the name directly. A variable that does not exist is empty.
variables.lesson.6: Inside double quotes, Bash replaces `$name` with its value. Inside single quotes, nothing is replaced: the text stays exactly as written. Put variables in double quotes when you use them, like `"$text"`. Without quotes, Bash splits the value into words, and extra spaces disappear.
variables.lesson.9: `$(command)` runs a command and puts its output in that place. This is called **command substitution**. You can store the output in a variable. `${#name}` gives the number of characters in a value.
variables.lesson.12: Bash stores values as text. To calculate, write the expression inside `$(( ))`. Inside, you can leave out the `$` before variable names. You can use `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%` (the remainder of a division). Bash calculates with whole numbers only: `/` drops the decimal part. Without the `$`, `(( ))` changes a variable: `(( count += 5 ))` adds `5` to `count`.
variables.card.1: `"$name"` or `"${name}"` uses the value, `${#name}` is its length
variables.card.2: `"..."` replaces variables, `'...'` keeps the text as written
variables.card.3: `word=$(echo "hi")` stores the output of a command
variables-2.explain: Inside single quotes, Bash replaces nothing. Use double quotes to get `Hi Bob`.
variables-3.prompt: This script should print Total: 15. Which line has the bug?
variables-3.explain: There must be no spaces around `=`. With spaces, Bash runs a command called `count`. Write `count=3`.
variables-4.prompt: Complete the code so it prints apples.
variables-4.explain: The braces show where the name ends. `$fruits` would look for a variable called `fruits`.
variables-5.explain: Only `x=10` creates a variable. `x = 10` runs a command called `x` and fails.
variables-6.explain: `${#word}` is the number of characters in the value. `banana` has 6 characters.
variables-7.prompt: The variables a=10 and b=4 exist. Build a line that prints Difference: 6.
variables-7.explain: `$(( ))` calculates: `a - b` is `10 - 4`, which is `6`. A single `$( )` would run a command instead.
variables-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the script prints 8.
variables-8.explain: Every variable must exist before you use it: `a` is `2`, `b` is `6`, and `c` is `6 + 2`, which is `8`.
variables-9.prompt: Match each expression with what it gives.
variables-9.pairs.1: the number of characters in the value
variables-10.explain: Bash calculates with whole numbers only. `/` drops the decimal part, so `17 / 5` is `3`.
variables-11.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 10.
variables-11.explain: Only `$(( ))` calculates. `n=n+3` stores the text `n+3`, and `$( )` runs a command.
variables-12.prompt: This script should print Hello, Ada. Which line has the bug?
variables-12.explain: Single quotes keep `$name` as text. Write `greeting="Hello, $name"` with double quotes.
arguments.title: Script arguments
arguments.summary: Read the arguments of a script with $1, $2, $# and "$@", move them with shift and set default values.
arguments.lesson.0: You can give a script values when you start it: `bash greet.sh Ada 36`. These values are the **arguments** of the script. Inside the script, `$1` is the first argument, `$2` the second, and so on. `$0` is the name of the script.
arguments.lesson.1: The examples on this page cannot use a command line, so they set the arguments with `set --`. The line `set -- Ada 36` works as if you started the script with the arguments `Ada` and `36`. In a real script, leave out this line.
arguments.lesson.3: `$#` is the number of arguments. An argument that was not given is empty. From the tenth argument on, you need braces: `${10}`.
arguments.lesson.6: `"$@"` stands for all arguments, each one as a separate word. Always write it with double quotes: then an argument with a space stays one argument. `"$*"` joins all arguments into one text, with spaces between them.
arguments.lesson.9: `shift` removes the first argument. The others move down: `$2` becomes `$1`, `$3` becomes `$2`, and `$#` gets one smaller. This is useful when the first argument is special, for example a command name.
arguments.lesson.12: `${1:-guest}` gives the value of `$1`, or the text `guest` when `$1` is empty or missing. This works with every variable, for example `${name:-nobody}`. `set --` without values removes all arguments.
arguments.card.0: `$1`, `$2` … are the arguments, `$0` is the script name
arguments.card.2: `"$@"` gives all arguments, each one separate
arguments-1.explain: `$#` is the number of arguments: `a`, `b`, `c` and `d`.
arguments-2.explain: `shift` removes `one`. Then `two` is the first argument.
arguments-3.explain: `$2` is `y` and `$1` is `x`. Nothing is between them, so the result is `yx`.
arguments-4.prompt: Which variable holds the number of arguments?
arguments-4.explain: `$#` is the count. `$@` gives the arguments themselves, `$0` is the script name and `$1` the first argument.
arguments-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hello, guest when there are no arguments.
arguments-5.explain: `${1:-guest}` gives `guest` when `$1` is empty or missing.
arguments-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3 files.
arguments-6.explain: `$#` is the number of arguments, here `3`. `$3` would be the third argument, `c.txt`.
arguments-7.statement: After `shift`, `$#` is one smaller than before.
arguments-7.explain: `shift` removes the first argument, so there is one argument less.
arguments-8.prompt: The script has the arguments tea milk. Build a line that prints milk and tea.
arguments-8.explain: `$2` is `milk` and `$1` is `tea`. The first `%s` gets `$2`, the second gets `$1`.
arguments-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the script prints add: 12.
arguments-9.explain: First set the arguments, then save `$1` before `shift` removes it. After `shift`, `$1` is `5` and `$2` is `7`.
arguments-10.prompt: Match each variable with its meaning.
arguments-10.pairs.4: the first argument, or x when it is empty
arguments-11.prompt: This script should print Hello, Ada and Bob. Which line has the bug?
arguments-11.explain: There are only two arguments, so `$3` is empty. Bob is the second argument: write `second=$2`.
arguments-12.prompt: This script should treat big apple as one argument and print 2 arguments. Which line has the bug?
arguments-12.explain: Without quotes, `big` and `apple` are two arguments. Write `set -- "big apple" pie`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Make decisions with if, test numbers and text in [[ ]], combine commands with && and ||, and choose with case.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs commands only when a condition is true. The test goes inside `[[ ]]`, with a space after `[[` and before `]]`. The `;` ends the test, `then` starts the commands, `else` starts the commands for a false test, and `fi` (`if` written backwards) ends the block.
conditions.lesson.3: For numbers, use `-eq` (equal), `-ne` (not equal), `-lt` (less than), `-le` (less or equal), `-gt` (greater than) and `-ge` (greater or equal). `elif` (else if) checks another condition when the first one is false. You can also compare numbers inside `(( ))` with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`.
conditions.lesson.6: For text, use `==` (equal) and `!=` (not equal). `-z` is true when a value is empty, and `-n` when it is not empty. On the right side of `==`, `*` is a pattern that matches any text: `[[ $file == *.jpg ]]` is true for every name that ends in `.jpg`.
conditions.lesson.8: `<` and `>` inside `[[ ]]` compare text in alphabetical order, not numbers. So `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` is true, because `1` comes before `9`. For numbers, use `-lt`, `-gt` or `(( ))`.
conditions.lesson.10: Every command ends with an **exit status**: `0` means success, any other number means failure. A test in `[[ ]]` has the status `0` when it is true. `a && b` runs `b` only when `a` succeeds. `a || b` runs `b` only when `a` fails. Inside `[[ ]]`, `&&` means and, `||` means or, and `!` turns true into false.
conditions.lesson.12: `case` compares one value with several patterns. Each pattern ends with `)`, and each branch ends with `;;`. `|` separates patterns that share a branch, and `*` matches everything else. `esac` (`case` written backwards) ends the block.
conditions.card.3: `a && b` runs `b` on success, `a || b` on failure
conditions-1.explain: `7 % 2` is `1`, not `0`, so the test is false and the `else` branch runs.
conditions-2.explain: `<` inside `[[ ]]` compares text: `10` comes before `9` in alphabetical order, because `1` comes before `9`.
conditions-3.prompt: Complete the code so it prints different.
conditions-3.explain: `!=` is true when two texts are not equal. `-ne` compares numbers, not text.
conditions-4.prompt: This script should print pass. Which line has the bug?
conditions-4.explain: Bash needs a space after `[[`. Without it, Bash looks for a command called `[[75`. Write `if [[ $score -ge 50 ]]; then`.
conditions-5.statement: The exit status `0` means that a command failed.
conditions-5.explain: `0` means success. Every other number means failure.
conditions-6.explain: The test is false, so `&&` skips `echo "big"`, and `||` runs `echo "small"`.
conditions-7.prompt: Build a line that prints no user when the variable user is empty.
conditions-7.explain: `-n` is true when the value is not empty. When the test fails, `||` runs the `echo`.
conditions-8.prompt: The variable age holds 20. Put the lines in order so the script prints adult.
conditions-8.explain: `20` is greater than or equal to `18`, so the line after `then` runs. The line after `else` runs only for a false test, and `fi` ends the block.
conditions-9.prompt: Match each test with its meaning.
conditions-9.pairs.1: a number is less than another
conditions-10.explain: `Sat` matches the second pattern. `;;` ends the branch, so `*)` does not run.
conditions-11.prompt: Complete the code so it prints one.
conditions-11.explain: `case` ends with `esac`, the word `case` written backwards.
conditions-12.prompt: This script should print b is bigger. Which line has the bug?
conditions-12.explain: `>` compares text, and `9` comes after `10` in alphabetical order. For numbers, write `if [[ $a -gt $b ]]; then`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat commands with for over lists and ranges, C-style for and while, and control loops with break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: `for` repeats commands for every word in a list. In each round, the variable gets the next word. The commands go between `do` and `done`.
loops.lesson.2: `{1..5}` creates the numbers from `1` to `5`. This is called **brace expansion**. A third number sets the step: `{1..10..3}` counts in steps of `3`. Letters work too: `{a..e}`.
loops.lesson.4: Brace expansion does not work with variables: with `n=3`, `{1..$n}` stays the text `{1..3}`. Use a C-style loop for that.
loops.lesson.6: `for (( i = 1; i <= n; i++ ))` has three parts: the start value, the condition, and the step. The loop runs while the condition is true. `i++` adds `1` to `i`.
loops.lesson.9: `while` repeats commands as long as a test is true. Make sure that something in the loop changes the test, or the loop never ends. `until` is the opposite: it repeats until the test becomes true.
loops.lesson.12: `break` leaves the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and starts the next one.
loops.card.0: `for x in a b c; do … done`
loops.card.2: `for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do … done`
loops.card.4: `break` leaves the loop, `continue` starts the next round
loops-1.explain: The loop adds `2`, `4` and `6` to `total`, which gives `12`.
loops-2.explain: `{1..10..3}` gives `1 4 7 10`, so the loop runs four times.
loops-3.explain: When `i` is `3`, `break` leaves the loop before `echo` runs. `1245` would be the result of `continue`.
loops-4.explain: Brace expansion happens before Bash replaces variables, so `{1..$n}` is not a range. The loop runs once with the text `{1..3}`.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 012.
loops-5.explain: The loop must stop before `3`, so the condition is `i < 3`. `-lt` does not work inside `(( ))`.
loops-6.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints the three colors.
loops-6.explain: The commands of a loop go between `do` and `done`. `then` belongs to `if`.
loops-7.explain: `continue` skips only the rest of the current round. `break` ends the whole loop.
loops-8.prompt: Build a loop that prints the numbers 1 to 5, one per line.
loops-8.explain: `for i in {1..5}` goes through the numbers, and `do` … `done` holds the command for each round.
loops-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the script prints 1, 2 and 3.
loops-9.explain: `n` must exist before the loop. Print `n` first and then add `1`, or the script prints `2`, `3` and `4`.
loops-10.prompt: Match each part with what it does.
loops-10.pairs.3: ends the body of a loop
loops-10.pairs.4: repeats while a test is true
loops-11.prompt: This script should print the sum of 1 to 4, which is 10. Which line has the bug?
loops-11.explain: After the loop, `i` holds the last number, `4`. The sum is in `sum`: write `echo "$sum"`.
loops-12.prompt: This script should print a, b and c, one per line. Which line has the bug?
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Group commands in functions, pass arguments, use local variables, return results and check exit codes with $?.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a group of commands with a name. You define it once with `name() { … }`, and then you call it by its name, like a command. Define a function before you call it.
functions.lesson.2: Functions get arguments like scripts do. Inside a function, `$1`, `$2`, `$#` and `"$@"` are the arguments of the function call.
functions.lesson.5: Variables in Bash are **global**: a function can read and change the variables of the whole script. `local` creates a variable that exists only inside the function. Use `local` for the variables of a function, unless you want to change a global variable.
functions.lesson.8: To give a value back, the function prints it with `echo`. The caller catches the output with `$( )`, like the output of any other command.
functions.lesson.11: `return` ends a function and sets its exit status. `0` means success, or yes. `$?` holds the exit status of the last command. Because `if` checks an exit status, you can use a function as the test of an `if`.
functions.lesson.13: `return` is not for results: it only gives an exit status from `0` to `255`. Use `echo` for real values. `$?` changes after every command, so read it right after the command you want to check.
functions.card.1: `$1`, `$#` and `"$@"` are the arguments of the function
functions.card.2: `local x=5` exists only inside the function
functions.card.4: `return 1` sets the exit status, `$?` reads it
functions-1.explain: `add 4 5` prints `9`, and `$( )` stores this output in `sum`.
functions-2.explain: `count` is global, so each call adds `10`: `1 + 10 + 10` is `21`.
functions-3.explain: Inside the function, `x` is local, so `x=3` changes only the local copy. The global `x` stays `1`.
functions-4.explain: `return 3` sets the exit status to `3`, and `$?` holds the status of the last command.
functions-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hi, Ada.
functions-5.explain: `$1` is the first argument of the function call, here `Ada`.
functions-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 100.
functions-6.explain: With `local`, the function creates its own `total`, and the global `total` keeps the value `100`.
functions-7.statement: You must define a function before you call it.
functions-7.explain: Bash runs a script from top to bottom. When it reaches a call, the function must already exist.
functions-8.prompt: Build a function dec that prints its argument minus 1.
functions-8.explain: The function prints the result of `$1 - 1` with `echo`. The `;` before `}` is needed when the body is on one line.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the script prints 8.
functions-9.explain: The function must be defined before the call. `3 > 8` is false, so the `else` branch prints `$2`, which is `8`.
functions-10.prompt: Match each part with its meaning.
functions-10.pairs.0: a variable only inside the function
functions-10.pairs.2: the exit status of the last command
functions-10.pairs.3: the output of the function f
functions-10.pairs.4: the first argument of the function
functions-11.prompt: This script should print Area: 12. Which line has the bug?
functions-11.explain: To catch the output of the function, use command substitution: `result=$(area 3 4)`.
functions-12.prompt: This script should print 4 is even. Which line has the bug?
functions-12.explain: The function returns `0` (yes) for odd numbers. An even number has the remainder `0`: write `if (( $1 % 2 == 0 )); then`.
text.title: Pipes and text
text.summary: Write files with > and >>, connect commands with pipes, and work with text using grep, sort, uniq, wc, cut and tr.
text.lesson.0: `>` sends the output of a command into a file instead of the screen. It creates the file, or overwrites it when it exists. `>>` adds the output to the end of a file. `cat` prints the content of a file.
text.lesson.2: A **here-doc** gives a command several lines of input. `<<EOF` starts it, and a line with only `EOF` ends it. Bash replaces variables inside. With `cat > note.txt <<EOF`, the lines go into a file.
text.lesson.5: The **pipe** `|` sends the output of one command to the next command as its input. `sort` sorts lines, `sort -r` sorts in reverse, and `sort -n` sorts numbers by their value. `uniq` removes a line when it repeats the line before it, so you usually sort first. `head -n 2` keeps the first two lines. `<` reads the input of a command from a file.
text.lesson.8: `grep word file` prints the lines that contain `word`. `-i` ignores the difference between capital and small letters, `-v` prints the lines that do not contain the word, and `-c` counts the matching lines.
text.lesson.11: `cut -d, -f1` splits each line at the character `,` and keeps field `1`. `tr a-z A-Z` replaces characters, here small letters with capital letters, and `tr -d " "` deletes all spaces. `wc -l` counts lines.
text.lesson.13: On some systems, `wc -l` prints spaces before the number. `tr -d " "` removes them, so your script prints the same everywhere.
text.card.0: `cmd > file` writes, `cmd >> file` appends, `cmd < file` reads
text.card.1: `cmd1 | cmd2` sends the output to the next command
text-1.explain: After `sort`, the two `a` lines are next to each other, and `uniq` keeps one of them: `a`, `b` and `c` are 3 lines.
text-2.explain: `cut -d,` splits the line at each `,`, and `-f3` keeps the third field.
text-3.explain: The second `>` overwrites the file, so `one` is gone. `>>` adds `three` at the end.
text-4.prompt: Which command prints the lines of log.txt that do not contain INFO?
text-4.explain: `-v` turns the search around: `grep` prints the lines that do not match.
text-5.prompt: Complete the code so it counts the lines with error, in capital or small letters. It should print 2.
text-5.explain: `-i` ignores the difference between capital and small letters, and `-c` counts the matching lines.
text-6.prompt: Complete the code so the file contains both lines.
text-6.explain: `>>` adds to the end of the file. `>` would overwrite the line `first`.
text-7.statement: `uniq` removes all repeated lines, even when they are not next to each other.
text-7.explain: `uniq` only removes a line that repeats the line right before it. Sort first with `sort | uniq`.
text-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the value of name in capital letters.
text-8.explain: The pipe sends the output of `echo` to `tr`, which replaces every small letter with the capital letter.
text-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the script prints apple, then pear.
text-9.explain: `>` creates the file and `>>` adds to it. Then `sort` writes the sorted lines to `sorted.txt`, and `cat` prints them.
text-10.prompt: Match each symbol or command with its meaning.
text-10.pairs.0: writes the output to a file
text-10.pairs.1: adds the output to the end of a file
text-10.pairs.2: reads the input from a file
text-10.pairs.3: sends the output to the next command
text-11.prompt: This script should print how many lines contain ERROR. Which line has the bug?
text-11.explain: `-v` counts the lines without `ERROR`. Remove it: `grep "ERROR" log.txt | wc -l | tr -d " "`.
text-12.prompt: This script should print each letter only once, in alphabetical order. Which line has the bug?
text-12.explain: `uniq` only removes repeated lines that are next to each other, so you must sort first: `sort letters.txt | uniq`.
arrays.title: Arrays
arrays.summary: Store lists in indexed arrays, loop over them, count their elements and use declare -A for arrays with text keys.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** stores several values in one variable. Create it with parentheses: `fruits=(apple banana cherry)`. Each value is an **element** with a number, its **index**. The index starts at `0`. To read an element, write `${fruits[0]}`, with braces.
arrays.lesson.2: `"${fruits[@]}"` gives all elements, each one as a separate word. `${#fruits[@]}` is the number of elements. `+=( )` adds elements at the end.
arrays.lesson.4: `$fruits` without an index gives only the first element. And without braces, `$fruits[1]` is the first element followed by the text `[1]`, so it prints `apple[1]`. Always write `${fruits[1]}`.
arrays.lesson.6: To go through all elements, write `for x in "${arr[@]}"`. Keep the double quotes: then an element with a space stays one element.
arrays.lesson.8: `"${!arr[@]}"`, with `!`, gives the indexes instead of the elements. Use it when you need the index and the element.
arrays.lesson.11: `declare -A` creates an **associative array**. Its keys are text instead of numbers, so you can store a value for every name. `${#ages[@]}` and `"${!ages[@]}"` work here too. This needs Bash 4 or newer.
arrays.lesson.13: The keys of an associative array come in no fixed order. When the order matters, sort them: `printf "%s\n" "${!ages[@]}" | sort`.
arrays.card.0: `arr=(a b c)`, `${arr[0]}` is the first element, `arr+=(d)` appends
arrays.card.1: `"${arr[@]}"` all elements, `${#arr[@]}` their number, `"${!arr[@]}"` the indexes
arrays-1.explain: The index starts at `0`: `4` has the index `0`, so `16` has the index `3`.
arrays-2.explain: `+=` adds two elements to the two that exist, so the array has 4 elements.
arrays-3.explain: Without an index, `$animals` gives only the first element. Use `"${animals[@]}"` for all elements.
arrays-4.explain: A key exists only once. The second `capital[France]=` replaces `Lyon`, so there are 2 keys.
arrays-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints all colors.
arrays-5.explain: `${colors[@]}` gives all elements. `0` and `1` give only one element.
arrays-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.
arrays-6.explain: `${#list[@]}` is the number of elements. `${!list[@]}` gives the indexes `0 1 2`.
arrays-7.statement: The first element of a Bash array has the index `1`.
arrays-7.explain: The index starts at `0`. `${arr[1]}` is the second element.
arrays-8.prompt: Build a loop that prints every element of names on its own line.
arrays-8.explain: `"${names[@]}"` gives all elements, and the loop prints each one.
arrays-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the script prints Hi, Ada, Hi, Bob and Hi, Eve.
arrays-9.explain: Create the array first, then add `Eve`, and then loop over all three elements.
arrays-10.prompt: Match each expression with its meaning.
arrays-10.pairs.4: creates an array with text keys
arrays-11.prompt: This script should print 4 colors. Which line has the bug?
arrays-11.explain: `${#colors}` is the length of the first element, `red`. For the number of elements, write `count=${#colors[@]}`.
arrays-12.prompt: This script should print Bob is 25. Which line has the bug?
arrays-12.explain: Without braces, Bash reads `$ages` and then the text `[Bob]`. Write `echo "Bob is ${ages[Bob]}"`.
